questions.stem: Translocation moves sucrose from 'sources' to 'sinks'. In a potato plant during the growing season, which structures act as sources and which as sinks?

options.text: Leaves are sources (produce sugar); developing tubers are sinks (receive sugar for storage)
Roots are sources; leaves are sinks
Tubers are sources; flowers are sinks
Every part of the plant is both a source and a sink

questions.explanation: Sources are parts of the plant that produce or release sugars -- mainly photosynthesising leaves. Sinks are parts that use or store sugars -- such as growing roots, developing tubers, fruits, and seeds. In spring, stored tubers can become sources as they release stored starch (converted to sucrose) to fuel new growth.

questions.stem: Phloem sieve tube elements have very few organelles and their end walls (sieve plates) have pores. How does this structure help their function?

options.text: Fewer organelles means more room for DNA storage
Fewer organelles leaves more space for the flow of sugary sap; sieve plate pores allow continuous flow between cells
The pores allow water to escape
Fewer organelles reduces the need for oxygen

questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements lose most of their organelles (including the nucleus) during development, maximising the internal space available for the flow of sucrose solution. The sieve plates have pores that allow the sugary sap to flow from one cell to the next in a continuous stream. Companion cells provide the metabolic support the sieve tubes need.

questions.stem: Unlike water movement in xylem, translocation in phloem requires energy (ATP). Why?

options.text: Sugar molecules are heavier than water
Sucrose is actively loaded into phloem sieve tubes at the source, and the pressure flow mechanism requires metabolic energy
Phloem has no way to generate pressure passively
Energy is needed to keep sieve tube cells alive

questions.explanation: At source cells, sucrose is actively loaded into phloem sieve tubes using ATP (from companion cells). This increases the solute concentration inside the phloem, causing water to enter by osmosis, building up pressure. This pressure drives the flow of sap toward sinks. The active loading step is what makes translocation an energy-requiring process.

questions.stem: Companion cells are found alongside sieve tube elements in phloem. They have many mitochondria. What does this suggest about their role?

options.text: They photosynthesise to produce sugars
They carry out aerobic respiration to produce ATP, providing energy for active loading of sucrose into sieve tubes
They transport water alongside the phloem
They store excess glucose as starch

questions.explanation: Companion cells have a dense cytoplasm packed with mitochondria, indicating a high rate of aerobic respiration. The ATP produced is used to actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements via membrane transport proteins. Since sieve tube elements lack most organelles (including a nucleus), companion cells provide the metabolic functions they cannot perform themselves.

questions.stem: Aphids (greenfly) feed by inserting their stylet (needle-like mouthpart) into phloem sieve tubes and drinking the sugary sap. Scientists have used this behaviour to study phloem transport. How?

options.text: They count how many aphids can feed on one plant
They anaesthetise the aphid and cut its stylet, allowing sap to continue flowing out for collection and analysis
They use aphids to inject radioactive tracers into phloem
They measure the weight of the aphid after feeding

questions.explanation: Scientists can anaesthetise a feeding aphid (often with CO2), then carefully cut its body away, leaving the stylet embedded in the phloem. Phloem sap continues to flow out through the stylet (driven by the pressure in the phloem) and can be collected for analysis. This technique was crucial in determining that phloem transports sucrose and amino acids.
